lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding trustworthy farm information
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Judge whether a piece of farm advice is trustworthy before acting on it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a piece of farm advice from a message, app or neighbour, you will check who says it, whether it fits your area and crop, whether it is recent and whether they are selling something, before spending money, and spotting any scam signs.
Farmers get advice from many places: extension officers, research institutes such as KALRO in Kenya, agricultural development programs in Nigeria's states, FAO and CGIAR centres, agrovets, radio and TV programs, SMS and app services, WhatsApp and Facebook groups, and neighbours. Some is excellent; some is wrong, out of date, or trying to sell you something.
Ask four questions about any advice: Who says it, and do they know (a research institute or trained officer, or an unknown account)? Is it for my area and crop? Is it recent? Are they selling something? Check important advice with a second trusted source before you spend money.
Watch for scams: fake seed and fertilizer, "miracle" products, fake jobs or grants that ask for a fee, and messages pretending to be a government program asking for your mobile money PIN. Buy inputs from registered dealers and report fakes to the right authority.
Step by step:
- Ask: who says it, and do they know?
- Ask: is it for my area and crop, and is it recent?
- Ask: are they selling something?
- Check with a second trusted source before spending money.
- Buy inputs from registered dealers; never share your PIN.
Words to know:
- Extension officer: a trained adviser from the government or a project who helps farmers.
- Research institute: an organisation that tests and develops farming methods and varieties, such as KALRO.
- Scam: a trick to take your money or information.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
Try it now: Find one piece of farm advice you saw recently (on radio, WhatsApp or from a seller). Answer the four questions about it, and check it with a second trusted source. Write whether you will act on it.
You can now judge whether farm advice is trustworthy and spot common scams.

check.q: Which question helps you judge a piece of farm advice?
options: How many people liked the post?
Is it for my area and crop, and is it recent?
check.why: Checking who says it, whether it fits your area and crop, and whether it is recent shows if advice is trustworthy.

check.q: A message says you won a farm grant and asks for your mobile money PIN. What do you do?
options: Treat it as a scam and do not share the PIN
Forward it to your group to apply
check.why: Real programs never ask for your PIN or a fee to release a grant.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Recording your farm's data on a phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set up a simple phone system to record plots, inputs, scouting and harvest.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free spreadsheet or form app on your phone, you will set up a farm data sheet with one row per event and a fixed name for each plot, with at least date, plot, activity, quantity and cost columns.
Your own records are the most valuable data you have, because they are about your farm. A spreadsheet app (Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel, both free on phones) works well: one row per event, with columns such as date, plot, crop, activity, quantity, cost and notes.
Give each plot a short name or number and keep it the same. Record a GPS point or a rough boundary for each plot (many map apps let you drop a pin and share its coordinates). Take photos of problems and name them with the date and plot. For groups and cooperatives, free form tools such as KoboToolbox let many members fill the same form on their phones, even offline, and send it when they get network.
Keep it simple enough to do every time. Five columns filled in every week are worth more than twenty columns filled in once. Back up the sheet (most cloud spreadsheets save automatically) and do not put private numbers such as PINs or ID numbers in it.
Step by step:
- Open a free spreadsheet app and make columns: date, plot, crop, activity, quantity, cost, notes.
- Name each plot and record a GPS pin for it.
- Add a row each time you plant, apply inputs, scout, harvest or sell.
- Name photos with date and plot.
- For groups: consider a shared form that works offline.
Words to know:
- Spreadsheet: a table of rows and columns on a phone or computer for recording and calculating.
- GPS pin: a saved point on a map with its coordinates.
- Offline: working without an internet connection.
Official sources:
- KoboToolbox (free data collection forms)
Try it now: Create your farm sheet on your phone with the seven columns. Add your plots and at least five rows of real activities from this season. Drop a GPS pin for one plot and save its coordinates in the notes.
You can now record your farm's activities, inputs and harvest on a phone in a consistent way.

check.q: In a farm data sheet, what is one row?
options: One event, such as a planting or a sale
check.why: One row per event, with date, plot, activity, quantity and cost, keeps records easy to add up.

check.q: Your farmer group wants members to send scouting reports from areas with poor network. What could you use?
options: A long phone call each week
Paper notes that stay at home
A different app for each member
A shared form tool such as KoboToolbox that works offline
check.why: Form tools like KoboToolbox let many members fill the same form offline and send it when they get network.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Using free weather and satellite information
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use official forecasts and free satellite maps to inform farm decisions.
This lesson builds toward: For your area and season, you will find the official weather forecast and a free satellite or rainfall map and record what they show in your farm sheet, with the source and the date.
National weather services publish forecasts for farmers: in Kenya, the Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) publishes seasonal forecasts and agrometeorological bulletins; in Nigeria, NiMet publishes seasonal climate predictions and forecasts. Note what they say for your area in your farm sheet, with the date, so you can later see how it matched your season.
Free satellite information helps too. FAO's earth observation pages show rainfall, vegetation (NDVI) and agricultural stress maps for countries and regions, useful to see whether a dry spell is local or widespread. The Copernicus Browser shows free Sentinel-2 satellite images every few days at about 10 metres per pixel, enough to see the shape of fields and whether a large field is greener or browner than last month.
If you can, measure rainfall yourself with a simple rain gauge and record it every day. Your own rainfall record, next to your planting dates and yields, quickly shows what works on your farm.
Step by step:
- Find your national weather service's forecast for your area.
- Write it in your farm sheet with the date.
- Look at FAO's earth observation maps for your country.
- Find your farm in the Copernicus Browser and compare two dates.
- Record daily rainfall with a simple gauge if you can.
Words to know:
- Agrometeorological bulletin: a weather report written for farmers.
- Satellite image: a picture of the earth taken from space.
- Rain gauge: a simple container with a scale that measures rainfall.
Official sources:
- Kenya Meteorological Department (forecasts and agrometeorological bulletins)
- Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet)
- FAO GIEWS Earth Observation (rainfall, NDVI and agricultural stress maps)
- Copernicus Browser (free Sentinel satellite images)
Try it now: Find this season's forecast for your area and write it in your farm sheet. Then find your area in FAO's earth observation maps or the Copernicus Browser and write one thing you notice.
You can now use official forecasts and free satellite maps alongside your own farm records.

check.q: Where do official seasonal forecasts for farmers in Nigeria come from?
check.why: NiMet publishes Nigeria's seasonal climate predictions and forecasts.

check.q: You want to know whether a dry spell is only on your farm or across the region. What do you check?
options: FAO's earth observation rainfall and vegetation maps
check.why: FAO's earth observation maps show rainfall, vegetation and stress for countries and regions.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Analysing your records in a spreadsheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate yield and profit per plot and make a chart to compare them.
This lesson builds toward: Given records for at least three plots, you will calculate yield and profit per acre with formulas, make a bar chart and write one decision for next season, with correct sums and the decision linked to the numbers.
Records become useful when you add them up. In your spreadsheet, make a summary table: one row per plot with its size, total cost, harvest, income, and then yield per acre and profit per acre. Spreadsheets do the maths with simple formulas, for example =SUM to add costs and a division to get yield per acre.
Then make a chart. Select the plot names and yield per acre (or profit per acre) and insert a bar chart. A chart makes differences easy to see and to explain to family, a group or a lender.
Look for reasons: did the best plot get manure, an earlier planting date, a different variety, or more rain? Did the weakest plot have pests or waterlogging? Write one decision for next season, and keep recording so you can test it.
Step by step:
- Make a summary table: plot, size, total cost, harvest, income.
- Use =SUM for totals and divide to get yield and profit per acre.
- Select plot names and yield per acre; insert a bar chart.
- Look for reasons in your notes.
- Write one decision for next season.
Words to know:
- Formula: an instruction in a spreadsheet cell that calculates, such as =SUM(B2:B10).
- Yield per acre: how much a plot produced divided by its size.
- Bar chart: a chart with bars that compare amounts.
Try it now: Make the summary table for at least three plots (real or example numbers), calculate yield and profit per acre with formulas, insert a bar chart, and write one decision for next season.
You can now analyse farm records in a spreadsheet and use a chart to compare plots and decide.

options: Income minus cost, divided by the plot size in acres
check.why: Profit per acre takes income minus cost and divides it by the plot size so plots of different sizes can be compared.

check.q: Your summary table shows one plot gave much more maize. What do you do next?
options: Look for reasons such as manure or planting date and write one decision
Delete the other plots from the sheet
Plant only that plot forever without checking
check.why: Finding the reasons and writing one decision you can test next season turns records into better farming.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Using AI assistants for farm questions, responsibly
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant a clear farm question and check the answer before acting.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will write a clear farm question and check the answer with extension, an agrovet or the label, before acting, and typing no private information.
Free AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini can explain farming ideas, help plan a season, draft a message to a buyer, translate, or help build a spreadsheet formula. Ask clearly: say your crop, area, season, farm size and what you want, for example: "I farm 2 acres of maize in Bungoma. The short rains start in October. Make me a simple weekly checklist from land preparation to harvest. Use short sentences."
AI can be wrong, out of date, or give advice for another country. It may name products not registered in your country or wrong rates. Never act on AI advice about pesticides, fertilizer rates, animal medicines or money without checking with your extension officer, agrovet, the product label or another trusted source.
Do not type private information into an AI assistant: your ID number, mobile money PIN, bank details or other people's personal data. Use AI as a helpful starting point, not the final word.
Step by step:
- Say your crop, area, season, farm size and what you want.
- Ask for short sentences or a checklist.
- Ask follow-ups to improve the answer.
- Check pesticide, fertilizer, medicine and money advice with a trusted source.
- Never type PINs, ID numbers or bank details.
Words to know:
- AI assistant: a computer program you chat with in everyday words that writes answers.
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant.
Try it now: Ask a free AI assistant for a weekly checklist for your main crop this season, using the prompt pattern from this lesson. Mark every item that needs checking with a trusted source, and check one of them.
You can now ask an AI assistant a clear farm question and check its answer before acting.

check.q: Which is a clear farm question for an AI assistant?
options: "I grow 1 acre of beans in Kakamega. The long rains start in March. Give me a short planting checklist."
check.why: It gives the crop, area, season, farm size and what you want.

check.q: An AI assistant gives you a fertilizer rate for your crop. What do you do?
options: Check it with your extension officer, agrovet or the label
Post it in your group as fact
check.why: AI can give wrong rates or advice for another country, so rates must be checked first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Protecting and sharing your farm data
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide what farm data to share, with whom, and keep the rest safe.
This lesson builds toward: When an app, buyer or group asks for farm data, you will decide what to share, with whom and why, and protect the rest, following your country's data protection rights and asking others for consent.
Your farm data has value: buyers, lenders, insurers, input companies and apps may want it. Sharing can help you get a loan, insurance or a contract, but you should know what you share, why and with whom. Read what an app or program says it will do with your data, and say no if you are not comfortable.
Data protection laws give you rights over your personal data. In Kenya, the Data Protection Act 2019 is overseen by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC); in Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 is overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). If you collect data from other farmers, for example as a group leader, you must also respect their rights: ask for consent and keep it safe.
Keep your phone and sheets safe: a screen lock, a strong password on your accounts, backups, and care with shared phones. Share summaries (such as yield per acre) rather than everything when that is enough.
Step by step:
- Before sharing, ask: what, why, with whom, and what do I get?
- Read the app's or program's data terms.
- Ask other farmers for consent before collecting their data.
- Lock your phone; use strong passwords; back up.
- Share summaries instead of all details when possible.
Words to know:
- Personal data: information about a person who can be identified.
- Consent: a clear yes after understanding what will happen with the data.
- Data protection law: a law that controls how personal data may be collected and used.
Official sources:
- Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (Kenya)
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
Try it now: Final task: complete your season farm data sheet for at least three plots, make one comparison chart, write one decision for next season, list the sources you checked, and write three steps you take to keep the data safe.
You can now collect, analyse, share and protect your farm data to make better decisions.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Farm data sheet Missing columns, or plots named differently in different rows. One row per event with date, plot, activity, quantity and cost, and fixed plot names, for at least three plots. Also has scouting notes, photos or GPS points linked to the plots. Weather and satellite notes No forecast or rainfall information. The official forecast or a satellite or rainfall map is noted with its source and date. Includes the learner's own rain gauge record next to the forecast. Analysis and chart No summary table, or sums are wrong. Yield and profit per acre are correct for each plot and shown in a bar chart. The chart is explained in one or two sentences to a group or lender. Decision for next season No decision, or it does not follow from the numbers. One clear decision linked to what the sheet shows. Says how next season's records will test the decision. Sources checked Advice from apps, AI or social media is used without checking. Notes which trusted sources were used to check advice, including any AI answer. Names a second source for each important piece of advice. Data kept safe The sheet holds PINs, ID numbers or other people's data without consent. No private numbers; a note on backups, the screen lock and what is shared with whom. Shows a short summary prepared for sharing instead of the whole sheet. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the sheet and check it again.

check.q: Which body oversees data protection in Kenya?
options: The Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC)
check.why: Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 is overseen by the ODPC.

check.q: A lender wants to see how your farm performs. What do you share?
options: A summary such as yield per acre, after reading how they will use it
check.why: A summary is often enough, and you should know what you share, why and with whom.
